power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}

# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = c("p > 0.05", "p < 0.05", "p < 0.05", 
"p ≥ 0.05"), Text = c("A non-significant Q (p > 0.05) indicated that the two estimates were statistically compatible -the sex difference was consistent across cohorts -whereas a significant Q (p < 0.05) indicated heterogeneity in the magnitude or direction of the sex effect.", 
"A non-significant Q (p > 0.05) indicated that the two estimates were statistically compatible -the sex difference was consistent across cohorts -whereas a significant Q (p < 0.05) indicated heterogeneity in the magnitude or direction of the sex effect.",

"None of the 12 variables in the echocardiographic models showed significant between-cohort heterogeneity after FDR correction (all FDR-adjusted heterogeneity p ≥ 0.05)."
)), row.names = c(NA, -4L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"
```

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p > 0.05", "p = 0.09", "p ≥ 0.05"), Sentence = c("A non-significant Q (p > 0.05) indicated that the two estimates were statistically compatible -the sex difference was consistent across cohorts -whereas a significant Q (p < 0.05) indicated heterogeneity in the magnitude or direction of the sex effect.", "Diabetes also showed associations in opposite directions across cohorts, but the corresponding heterogeneity did not remain significant after FDR correction (OR = 1.19 versus 0.85; FDR-adjusted heterogeneity p = 0.09).", "None of the 12 variables in the echocardiographic models showed significant between-cohort heterogeneity after FDR correction (all FDR-adjusted heterogeneity p ≥ 0.05)." )), row.names = c(NA, -3L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

text.text: Sex differences in sudden cardiac arrest (SCA) incidence and outcomes are well established, but risk stratification underperforms in women.
It is important to delineate sex-specific patterns in SCA across clinical, electrocardiographic, and echocardiographic domains.

We studied out-of-hospital SCA cases from the Oregon Sudden Unexpected Death Study (ORSUDS; Portland, 2002-2020; discovery) and Prediction of Sudden Death in Multi-Ethnic Communities (PRESTO; Ventura County, 2015-2024; external replication).
Sex differences in 38 comorbidities, 19 ECG and 12 echocardiographic measures were estimated using multivariableadjusted logistic regression.
Female sex was the modeled dependent measure (male as reference).
ORSUDS estimates were compared with those in the Framingham Heart Study (FHS), a community-based reference cohort, using FDR-adjusted Cochran Q tests.
Among 5130 ORSUDS cases, 1715 (33.4%) were women (median age, 70.4 years [IQR, 58.7-81.8]) and 3415 (66.6%) were men (65.6 [55.0-76.8]).

Sudden cardiac arrest (SCA) remains a major contributor to cardiovascular mortality despite advances in prevention, emergency response, and post-arrest care.
Sex differences in epidemiology of SCA have been consistently reported across community-based and nationwide cohorts.

Men experience substantially higher SCA incidence than women across most adult age groups, although this difference narrows with advancing age. [1] [2] [3] [4] These differences suggest that sex is an important determinant of SCA risk, and women who have SCA may have clinical characteristics that differ from those observed in men. 5 Women are generally older at the time of arrest, less likely to have documented coronary artery disease (CAD) or severe left ventricular systolic dysfunction, and are more likely to present with non-shockable rhythms, unwitnessed events, and arrest at home. [6] [7] [8] [9] [10] Autopsy-based studies have also reported that women have less obstructive CAD and a higher proportion of nonischemic myocardial disease, myocardial fibrosis, or non-cardiac causes. 11, 12 However, other cohort studies have identified conventional cardiovascular risk factors, including hypertension, diabetes, smoking, obesity or central adiposity, prior myocardial infarction (MI), heart failure (HF), left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH), and QT-related abnormalities, as important predictors of sudden cardiac death (SCD) in women. [13] [14] [15] These findings indicate that traditional cardiovascular risk factors remain relevant in women, but their distribution and clinical expression may differ from those in men.

text.text: Therefore, comprehensive studies of sex differences in SCA are needed with evaluation of detailed clinical comorbidity profiles, prearrest electrocardiographic features, and echocardiographic findings.

Such analyses should be externally validated to determine whether sex differences among SCA cases are specific to SCA or whether they simply reflect background sex differences present in the community population.

To address this knowledge gap, we evaluated sex-associated SCA profiles before the index event, across three domains: clinical comorbidities, electrocardiographic measures, and echocardiographic findings.

We used the Oregon Sudden Unexpected Death Study (ORSUDS) as the discovery cohort and the Prediction of Sudden Death in Multi-Ethnic Communities (PRESTO) study as an external replication cohort, with the Framingham Heart Study (FHS) serving as a community-cohort reference.

We hypothesized that SCA cases exhibit reproducible sex-associated profiles across clinical, electrical, and structural modalities, and that selected sex differences among SCA cases diverge from sex patterns observed in a community cohort.
For discovery, we utilized the ORSUDS study, which involved 5854 SCA cases occurring between 2002 and 2020 in the Portland, Oregon metro area.
This is an ongoing community-based study encompassing a catchment population of about 1 million.
The methodology, detailed elsewhere, 6, 16, 17 involves identifying SCA cases through emergency medical services (EMS), including ambulance and fire department first responders.

text.text: For each potential SCA case, medical history was retrieved from medical records, EMS narratives, and autopsy findings when available.

A panel of three physicians adjudicated the SCA cases using the following definition: SCA was a sudden, pulseless collapse due to a likely cardiac etiology, occurring rapidly after symptom onset when witnessed or if unwitnessed, within 24 h of the individual being last seen in their usual state of health. 18 Non-cardiac causes-such as trauma, drowning, overdose, terminal illness, active malignancies, or extracardiac causes like pulmonary embolism and other natural causes-were systematically excluded.

text.text: To comprehensively evaluate sex differences among SCA cases, we employed three complementary analytic approaches: (1) demographic and comorbidity characteristics; (2) ECG measures among SCA cases with a pre-event ECG; and (3) echocardiographic findings among SCA cases with a pre-event echocardiogram.
The specific variables included in each approach are detailed in the Supplementary methods.
Variables with more than 20% missingness were excluded.

To assess the generalizability and robustness of our findings, we performed an external replication using data from the ongoing PRESTO study from February 1, 2015, to January 31, 2024, which covers a catchment population of ~850,000 in Ventura County, CA.

In this study, SCA cases were identified using methods similar to those employed in the ORSUDS study, including consistent approaches to case ascertainment, adjudication, inclusion criteria, data retrieval, and SCA definitions.
The methodology of the PRESTO study has been described in previously published studies.
For the validation population, we selected SCA cases aged 18 years or older with comprehensive medical records, including ECG and echocardiography results obtained prior to SCA.

As the community cohort referent, we used the Offspring cohort of the Framingham Heart Study (FHS), a prospective, multigenerational epidemiological study designed to identify factors that contribute to cardiovascular disease.

The study methodology and participant selection criteria have been described previously. [19] [20] [21] The Offspring cohort, started in 1971, comprised 5124 individuals, including the children of the Original Cohort and the spouses of those children.

text.text: In this case-case analysis, initial univariable analyses were conducted without imputation.

Continuous variables were presented as mean ± standard deviation (SD) and, where appropriate, median with interquartile range (IQR), while categorical variables were reported as counts and percentages.
Group comparisons employed the chi-square test for proportions and either Student's t test or the Mann-Whitney U test for continuous variables, as appropriate.

To obtain adjusted ORs accounting for potential confounders, we performed multivariable logistic regression with female sex as the dependent measure (vs male sex), with multiple imputations via chained equations (MICE; R package mice) to address missing data.

Predictive mean matching was used to impute continuous variables, and logistic regression was applied to impute binary variables; the number of imputed datasets (m) was set to 10 to enhance robustness.

All variables within each analytic approach were included in the multivariable models, which were fit across all 10 imputed datasets; the numbers of covariates were 38 for demographic and clinical, 19 for ECG, and 12 for echo.
Final adjusted ORs and their 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were derived by pooling results across the imputed datasets to reduce uncertainty and bias.
For each feature, we estimated the female-versus-male log OR and its standard error separately in ORSUDS, PRESTO, and FHS.
We assessed heterogeneity in the sex association across the three cohorts using Cochran's 𝑄test.

text.text: In this community-based study, we identified distinct pre-arrest profiles among women and men with SCA across three complementary domains: clinical profile, ECG features, and echocardiographic findings.
SCA in women was more strongly associated with non-cardiac comorbidities, LVH, preserved LVEF, and mitral valve abnormalities.
In contrast, SCA in men was characterized by a greater burden of cardiac disease, behavioral risk factors, major ECG abnormalities, and left ventricular systolic dysfunction.

These patterns were externally validated in PRESTO, with 95.1% of tested associations showing no significant FDR-adjusted betweencohort heterogeneity, supporting their reproducibility across geographically and demographically distinct SCA populations.

In contrast, approximately half of the sex-associated differences observed among SCA cases diverged from corresponding sex patterns in the community cohort, the Framingham Heart Study: about one-quarter were directionally discordant, and another onequarter differed primarily in magnitude.

The observed heterogeneity between the SCA and community cohorts suggest that the observed sex-associated SCA profiles do not simply reflect background population differences but may instead represent potentially distinct pathways of SCD vulnerability in women versus men.

Specifically, women with SCA were older and demonstrated a broader non-cardiac comorbidity profile, with higher burdens of endocrine, immune, respiratory, pain-related, and neuropsychiatric conditions.

Although several of these conditions have an established female predominance in the general population, their association with female sex among SCA casesparticularly thyroid disease, autoimmune disease, asthma, chronic pain, dementia, and mood disorder-has not been comprehensively described and represents a novel contribution of this study.
Some of these associations may partly reflect background population sex differences, whereas others may be more characteristic of the clinical profile preceding SCA.
Female cases also had more frequent ECG-defined LVH.

The LVH finding is also consistent with the Fingesture study, in which LVH was the only ECG abnormality more common among women with SCD. 12 Our study extends this observation by demonstrating female enrichment of LVH on both ECG and echocardiography.

text.text: Female cases were also more likely to have preserved LVEF and mitral valve abnormalities, consistent with prior SCA studies reporting less severe left ventricular systolic dysfunction among women. 26 Collectively, these findings define a SCA for women with SCA characterized by non-cardiac comorbidities, hypertrophic remodeling, and preserved systolic function, which may be less readily recognized by conventional SCA profiles centered on documented CAD and reduced LVEF.

text.text: In contrast, men with SCA were characterized by a predominantly cardiovascular-arrhythmic phenotype across the clinical, electrical, and structural domains.

Clinically, male cases had greater burdens of CAD, AF, peripheral vascular disease, and sleep apnea, together with greater exposure to behavioral risk factors, particularly heavy alcohol and illicit drug use.

The predominance of CAD is consistent with previous studies, in which ischemic heart disease was more common among men than women with SCD. 3, 4, 6, 12, 27 To our knowledge, although they are recognized risk factors for SCA, peripheral vascular disease and sleep apnea have not previously been emphasized as sex-associated features among SCA cases and therefore represent potentially novel components of the male clinical phenotype.

text.text: The greater prevalence of sleep apnea in men with SCA despite significantly lower BMI than women with SCA could be partly explained by previous reports of more vulnerable anatomical and physiological characteristics (thick neck circumference and high neck-to-height ratio) relevant to sleep apnea along with established male predominance in the general population, 28, 29 whereas the enrichment of peripheral vascular disease may indicate broader vascular vulnerability relevant to SCA or may be influenced by under-recognition of vascular disease in women because of less typical clinical presentation. 30 From the electrophysiological perspective, male cases were more likely to have prolonged PR, prolonged QTc, premature contractions, and bradycardia.

text.text: The prolonged-QTc finding is consistent with Fingesture, which also reported higher prevalence of QTc prolongation and QRS abnormalities among men; 12 our findings for prolonged PR and premature contractions extend the previously described electrical profile.

text.text: Together, these electrical abnormalities are compatible with a greater burden of conduction-system disease, myocardial injury, and adverse remodeling among male cases.
Echocardiographic findings further reinforced this pattern: male cases were more likely to have reduced LVEF and segmental wall-motion abnormalities.

Collectively, these observations indicate that male SCA cases more often had recognized cardiovascular disease, electrical abnormalities, and systolic dysfunction before arrest-a pattern compatible with ischemic injury.
Comparison with FHS identified several sex-associated features whose patterns among SCA cases differed from those in the community cohort samples.
The clearest divergence involved prevalence of prolonged QTc, which was male-enriched in both SCA cohorts but femaleenriched in FHS.

This finding is consistent with an early analysis reported from the ORSUDS study that evaluated determinants of QTc prolongation in a control group of individuals with coronary disease but no history of SCA. 31 One possible explanation is that the greater burden of ischemic heart disease and left ventricular systolic dysfunction among male SCA cases may be accompanied by myocardial injury, adverse remodeling, and altered ventricular repolarization.

text.text: ECG-defined LVH showed a complementary divergence: it was strongly female-associated in both SCA cohorts but tended to be male-associated in the FHS cohort.

This finding is consistent with Fingesture, which reported a higher prevalence of ECG-LVH among women with SCD which was partly explained by the greater prevalence of primary myocardial fibrosis among women, raising the possibility that hypertrophic or fibrotic remodeling may contribute more prominently to the phenotype of women with SCA. 12 Higher BMI also showed a directional reversal, being female-enriched in ORSUDS but male-enriched in FHS.

text.text: One possible explanation is that male SCA cases more often exhibited ischemic heart disease and systolic dysfunction, which may be accompanied by disease-related weight loss and loss of lean mass, whereas female cases may be relatively enriched for obesity-related metabolic pathways.

The latter is supported by a UK Biobank study in which the triglyceride-glucose-BMI index showed a stronger association with incident SCA in women than in men. 32 This index reflects insulin resistance and metabolic burden, however, and does not establish a sex-specific effect of BMI itself.

text.text: Hypertension and HF were also female-directed in both SCA cohorts but male-enriched in FHS.

Together with the female enrichment of preserved LVEF and ECG defined LVH among SCA cases, this finding raises the possibility of a hypertrophic, preserved-EF phenotype among women which could be attributed to pressure overload.

Moreover, several additional clinical, ECG, and echocardiographic features showed sex associations in the same direction in ORSUDS and FHS, but the magnitudes of these associations differed significantly between the two populations.
For some features, the sex association was stronger among SCA cases, whereas for others it was stronger in FHS.
These findings suggest that pathophysiologic mechanism associated with SCA may modify the strength of sex differences observed in the general population.
Collectively, our findings represent the first step in a three-stage strategy toward sex-specific SCA risk prediction.
The first step is to establish whether women and men with SCA exhibit distinct pre-arrest profiles.

The external reproducibility of these profiles and the divergence of selected features from corresponding community patterns provide evidence that clinically meaningful sex differences exist among SCA cases and identify candidate features for subsequent risk-factor studies.
The second step is to determine whether these candidate features are associated with incident SCA differently in women and men.

Previous women-focused studies have identified hypertension, diabetes, smoking, adiposity, prior MI, HF, LVH, and QT-related measures as predictors of SCA. [13] [14] [15] However, comprehensive direct comparisons of the magnitude of these associations between women and men within the same source population remain limited.
text.formatted: Previous women-focused studies have identified hypertension, diabetes, smoking, adiposity, prior MI, HF, LVH, and QT-related measures as predictors of SCA. <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[14]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[15]</ref> However, comprehensive direct comparisons of the magnitude of these associations between women and men within the same source population remain limited.

text.text: Such studies should compare women with and without SCA and men with and without SCA and formally test sex-by-feature interactions to determine whether each condition has a similar, stronger, weaker, or potentially opposite association with SCA by sex.
The third and final step is to incorporate the resulting sex-specific risk factors into separate prediction models for women and men.

Unlike a single model developed in a combined-sex population, [33] [34] [35] separate models could use different predictors, predictor weights, thresholds, interactions, and nonlinear relationships that reflect the distinct profiles identified in the present study.
text.formatted: Unlike a single model developed in a combined-sex population, <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">[33]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">[34]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">[35]</ref> separate models could use different predictors, predictor weights, thresholds, interactions, and nonlinear relationships that reflect the distinct profiles identified in the present study.

text.text: The longterm objective is not simply to add sex as another variable to an existing SCA risk score, but to determine whether women and men require different predictors, different predictor weights, and ultimately different prediction models.

The present study defines the sex-associated profiles needed to begin that process; subsequent studies must identify the corresponding sex-specific risk factors and translate them into externally validated risk scores.
Several limitations should also be considered.

First, the primary case-case design in discovery cohort characterizes features associated with male versus female sex among individuals who experienced SCA; it cannot estimate sex-specific incident SCA risk, establish causal relationships, or determine the predictive value of the identified features.
Second, FHS is a predominantly White, New England-based cohort, with most participants having a high school or greater education, which may limit the generalizability to the general population.
Differences between FHS and ORSUDS participant selection and data-collection procedures may also have contributed to the observed heterogeneity, though findings were largely similar.
Third, some features were unavailable or not identically defined across ORSUDS and FHS, and the cohort-specific models consequently differed in their covariate composition.

Therefore, significant ORSUDS-FHS heterogeneity may partly reflect differences in measurement, variable availability, or model specification in addition to true differences between SCA cases and the reference cohort.
Fourth, our findings were observational and we cannot exclude residual confounding.
Fifth, although we used multiple imputations to address missing data, we acknowledge that the missing covariates may not have been missing at random.
Finally, for SCA cases pre-arrest ECG and echocardiographic data were available only in clinically selected subsets and were obtained at varied intervals before SCA.
This may have introduced selection and temporal measurement bias and may limit the generalizability of those findings to the entire SCA population.
Despite those limitations, this study has several important strengths.

To our knowledge, it is the first community-based investigation to comprehensively characterize pre-arrest sex-associated profiles across clinical, ECG, and echocardiographic domains, evaluate their reproducibility in a geographically and demographically distinct SCA cohort, and formally compare them with a community-based reference cohort.
The use of physician-adjudicated SCA cases, multivariableadjusted models, independent external replication in PRESTO, and FDR-adjusted Cochran Q tests strengthened the robustness of the analyses.
In addition, ORSUDS and PRESTO included a combined 2699 women with SCA, providing substantial female representation relative to most previous SCA studies.
Women and men with SCA exhibited distinct pre-arrest profiles across clinical, ECG, and echocardiographic domains which were broadly reproducible in two separate SCA cohorts, ORSUDS and PRESTO.
In contrast, many specific associations differed from corresponding sex patterns in the community-based FHS cohort.

By defining and externally validating these sexassociated phenotypes, this study lays the foundations for identifying sex-specific SCA risk factors and ultimately developing and validating sex-specific prediction models toward the ultimate goal of enhancing SCA risk stratification and prevention.
What is new?

 This study is the first community-based analysis to comprehensively characterize prearrest sex-associated profiles across clinical, ECG, and echocardiographic domains, externally validate them, and compare them with a community reference population.

 Women with SCA were more strongly associated with non-cardiac comorbidities, LVH, preserved LVEF, and mitral valve abnormalities, whereas male cases were characterized by coronary and peripheral vascular disease, atrial fibrillation, prolonged PR and QTc intervals, premature contractions, and reduced LVEF.
 Several sex associations, including QTc prolongation, LVH, body mass index, heart failure, and dementia, differed in magnitude or direction from patterns in the community reference population.
 Our findings suggest candidate features for future sex specific risk factor analyses and potential components for sex-specific risk models for SCA.
 Clinicians may need to recognize the critical need to extend beyond dependence on just the value of the left ventricular ejection fraction for SCA risk prediction, especially in women.
